title: Drona's student across the field
hook: Duryodhana jabs his teacher Drona, and why Hindus honor the acharya.
carry: honor the teacher: acharya devo bhava
tomorrow: why does Krishna get so many names in one chapter?

segments.voice: Yesterday, two princes looked at the same field, and we kept: moha clouds the eye; the Gita clears it. Duryodhana looked first. Now he walks up to his teacher and opens his mouth.

Picture a teacher who knew one of his students had been born to bring him down, and taught him anyway. That teacher is Drona, master of arms to the whole royal family. The Mahabharata tells that King Drupada, Drona's old friend turned enemy, prayed for a son who would defeat Drona, and a son came: Dhrishtadyumna. Drona took the boy in as a student all the same. Now it's the morning of the war. That student has arranged the army facing Drona, and Prince Duryodhana, another of Drona's students, walks up to him with one word: pashya. Look.
screen: `BORN TO DEFEAT HIS TEACHER.` → `TAUGHT ANYWAY.` → `PASHYA: LOOK.`

segments.voice: Here's his line: pashyaitam panduputranam acharya mahatim chamum. Look, O teacher, at this great army of Pandu's sons. Then the sting, saved for last: vyudham drupadaputrena tava shishyena dhimata. Drawn up by Drupada's son, your student, the wise one. Your student. Duryodhana could have said the enemy commander. He says the boy you trained. Some readers hear worry in it; many hear a prince needling the man who taught his enemy. Either way, he turns a teacher's gift into a jab. And that cuts against something Hindus hold very dear. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher sends his students home with a short charge: treat your mother as a god, your father as a god, your teacher as a god, your guest as a god. Acharya devo bhava. That's why many Hindu families teach children to touch a teacher's feet, and why Guru Purnima, a full-moon day in summer, is kept to thank teachers. In the tradition, knowledge is a gift, and the giver is honored. Drona gave it even to the boy born to defeat him. Duryodhana, his own student, says acharya and then mocks what the acharya gave. The first words anyone speaks on that field are a student failing his teacher. Today the honor can be simple and still hard: thanking the people who taught us, even when what they taught ended up helping someone we'd rather not see win.
screen: `LOOK, O TEACHER: YOUR STUDENT.` · `A GIFT TURNED INTO A JAB.` · `ACHARYA DEVO BHAVA: TEACHER AS GOD.` · `GURU PURNIMA: THANKING TEACHERS.` · then, large: `HONOR THE TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus begin study, or a recital, with a small bow to the teacher. Bring to mind one teacher from your life: a parent, a coach, someone who taught you a prayer. If you pray, join your palms, bow your head a little, and say their name with thanks. If you don't pray, simply picture their face and say thank you silently. Then rest with the breath, and let the words keep you company: acharya devo bhava.
Acharya: teacher. Duryodhana uses it to needle. The Upanishad says to honor it like a god.
Carry this: honor the teacher: acharya devo bhava. Drona taught even the boy born to defeat him. See you tomorrow.
